question: We hired temps to clear a backlog of customer complaints; the temps gave sloppy answers, which caused even more complaints. What pattern is this?
text:
This scenario is a classic example of the "Fixes That Fail" (also referred to as "Fixes That Backfire") system archetype[1][2].
In system dynamics, this archetype describes a situation where an urgent problem symptom is met with a short-term patch; while the patch may seem effective initially, it generates unintended consequences that ultimately make the original problem worse[2][3].
Structure of the Pattern
Problem Symptom: A heavy backlog of unresolved customer complaints[2][3].
Short-Term Fix: Hiring temporary staff (temps) to clear the queue quickly[2][3].
Unintended Consequence: Temps lack full training or familiarity with the system, leading to sloppy or inaccurate responses[2][3].
Reinforcing Feedback Loop: The sloppy answers anger customers further, generating a wave of new complaints and enlarging the backlog[2][3].
Related Pattern: "Shifting the Burden"
This scenario also connects to the "Shifting the Burden" archetype[1][4]. Relying on temporary fixes (bringing in short-term labor) treats the symptom rather than addressing fundamental solutions—such as improving root-cause product/service issues, refining training programs, or expanding permanent capacity[4]. Over time, relying on the quick fix can impede the organization's ability or incentive to invest in those lasting, upstream solutions[4].

An example of the “fixes that fail” archetype tells the story of exclusionary discipline in schools. Imagine a child who had a difficult morning at home, did not eat breakfast and arrived late to school. She is disruptive in class. A short-term solution for the teacher would be to send the child to time-out, suspension, or the principal’s office for the rest of the day. The teacher is employing a short-term fix; they are removing the disruption from the classroom. 4.chunk:
Archetype #3: Shifting the burden
The “shifting the burden” archetype shows what happens when we address the symptoms of a problem with a quick-fix solution. This solution is easier and faster than creating an upstream solution to the problem, and we are often meeting a very real, urgent need for a student. However, the quick-fix to the symptoms may actually impede our ability to invest time and energy to the fundamental solution. This makes it even harder to apply a fundamental solution and even more tempting to rely on quick fixes. Thus, the problem cannot be completely solved.
